raw: Act 3, Scene 2 — A Room in Capulet’s House
Enter Juliet.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds,
Towards Phoebus’ lodging. Such a waggoner
As Phaeton would whip you to the west
And bring in cloudy night immediately.
Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night,
That runaway’s eyes may wink, and Romeo
Leap to these arms, untalk’d of and unseen.
Lovers can see to do their amorous rites
By their own beauties: or, if love be blind,
It best agrees with night. Come, civil night,
Thou sober-suited matron, all in black,
And learn me how to lose a winning match,
Play’d for a pair of stainless maidenhoods.
Hood my unmann’d blood, bating in my cheeks,
With thy black mantle, till strange love, grow bold,
Think true love acted simple modesty.
Come, night, come Romeo; come, thou day in night;
For thou wilt lie upon the wings of night
Whiter than new snow upon a raven’s back.
Come gentle night, come loving black-brow’d night,
Give me my Romeo, and when I shall die,
Take him and cut him out in little stars,
And he will make the face of heaven so fine
That all the world will be in love with night,
And pay no worship to the garish sun.
O, I have bought the mansion of a love,
But not possess’d it; and though I am sold,
Not yet enjoy’d. So tedious is this day
As is the night before some festival
To an impatient child that hath new robes
And may not wear them. O, here comes my Nurse,
And she brings news, and every tongue that speaks
But Romeo’s name speaks heavenly eloquence.

sentences.en: I wish this day would end!
Gallop fast, you fiery horses of the sun, and pull it west.
A driver like Phaeton would whip you west and bring in a cloudy night immediately.
Spread your close curtain, love-performing night, so that prying eyes may close.
Then Romeo can leap into my arms, unseen and untalked of.
Lovers can see to perform their romantic acts by their own beauty.
Or if love is blind, it fits best with the night.
Come, serious night; you are like a serious older woman, all in black.
Teach me how to lose a game that I win by losing.
In it, two virgins give themselves to each other.
Hide the shy blood rushing to my cheeks with your black cloak until my shy love grows bold.
Then it will see that true love is pure.
Come, night, come Romeo; come, you day in the night.
You will lie on the wings of night and be whiter than new snow on a raven's back.
Come gentle night, come loving black-brow'd night, and give me my Romeo.
And when I die, take him and cut him into little stars.
He will make the face of heaven so fine.
All the world will be in love with the night.
No one will worship the bright sun.
Oh, I have bought the house of a love, but I do not possess it yet.
And though I have been sold to him, he has not yet enjoyed me.
This day is as tedious as the night before a festival to an impatient child with new clothes.
The child cannot wear them yet.
Look, here comes my Nurse, and she brings news.
Anyone who even says Romeo's name sounds like heaven to me.

raw: Enter Nurse, with cords.

sentences.en: The Nurse enters with ropes.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Now, Nurse, what news? What hast thou there?
The cords that Romeo bid thee fetch?

sentences.en: Now, Nurse, what news?
What do you have there?
Are these the ropes that Romeo told you to fetch?

speaker: NURSE
raw: Ay, ay, the cords.

sentences.en: Yes, yes, the ropes.

raw: Throws them down.

sentences.en: The Nurse throws them down.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Ay me, what news? Why dost thou wring thy hands?

sentences.en: Oh me, what news?
Why do you wring your hands?

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Ah, well-a-day, he’s dead, he’s dead, he’s dead!
We are undone, lady, we are undone.
Alack the day, he’s gone, he’s kill’d, he’s dead.

sentences.en: Oh, no, he is dead.
He is dead, he is dead!
We are ruined, lady, we are ruined.
Alas, the day, he is gone.
He is killed, he is dead.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Can heaven be so envious?

sentences.en: Can heaven be so cruel?

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Romeo can,
Though heaven cannot. O Romeo, Romeo.
Who ever would have thought it? Romeo!

sentences.en: Romeo can, even though heaven cannot.
Oh Romeo, Romeo, who ever would have thought it? Romeo!

speaker: JULIET
raw:
What devil art thou, that dost torment me thus?
This torture should be roar’d in dismal hell.
Hath Romeo slain himself? Say thou but Ay,
And that bare vowel I shall poison more
Than the death-darting eye of cockatrice.
I am not I if there be such an I;
Or those eyes shut that make thee answer Ay.
If he be slain, say Ay; or if not, No.
Brief sounds determine of my weal or woe.

sentences.en: What devil are you that you torment me like this?
This torture should be shouted in dark hell.
Has Romeo killed himself?
Say only 'Yes' to me.
That one little 'yes' will poison me more than a monster that kills with one look.
If you say 'yes', I am no longer myself.
If his eyes are closed forever, say 'yes'.
If he is killed, say 'Yes'.
If he is not, say 'No'.
Short sounds decide my happiness or my sadness.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
I saw the wound, I saw it with mine eyes,
God save the mark!—here on his manly breast.
A piteous corse, a bloody piteous corse;
Pale, pale as ashes, all bedaub’d in blood,
All in gore-blood. I swounded at the sight.

sentences.en: I saw the wound and I saw it with my own eyes.
God forgive me for saying it!
It was here on his manly chest.
A pitiful body, a bloody and pitiful body.
He was pale as ashes and covered in blood.
He was all in gore-blood.
I fainted at the sight.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
O, break, my heart. Poor bankrout, break at once.
To prison, eyes; ne’er look on liberty.
Vile earth to earth resign; end motion here,
And thou and Romeo press one heavy bier.

sentences.en: Oh, break my heart.
My poor heart, you have lost everything, so break now.
To prison, eyes; never look on liberty.
My body, go back to the earth.
Stop moving now.
Lie with Romeo in one coffin.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
O Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had.
O courteous Tybalt, honest gentleman!
That ever I should live to see thee dead.

sentences.en: Oh Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had.
Oh courteous Tybalt, honest gentleman!
That I should live to see you dead.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
What storm is this that blows so contrary?
Is Romeo slaughter’d and is Tybalt dead?
My dearest cousin, and my dearer lord?
Then dreadful trumpet sound the general doom,
For who is living, if those two are gone?

sentences.en: What storm is this that blows from both directions?
Is Romeo killed and is Tybalt dead?
My dearest cousin and my dearer lord?
Then let the terrible trumpet sound the final doom.
For who is living if those two are gone?

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Tybalt is gone, and Romeo banished,
Romeo that kill’d him, he is banished.

sentences.en: Tybalt is gone, and Romeo is banished, sent away from the city forever.
Romeo killed him, and he is banished.

speaker: JULIET
raw: O God! Did Romeo’s hand shed Tybalt’s blood?

sentences.en: Oh God!
Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?

speaker: NURSE
raw: It did, it did; alas the day, it did.

sentences.en: It did, it did, and what a terrible day!
It did.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
O serpent heart, hid with a flowering face!
Did ever dragon keep so fair a cave?
Beautiful tyrant, fiend angelical,
Dove-feather’d raven, wolvish-ravening lamb!
Despised substance of divinest show!
Just opposite to what thou justly seem’st,
A damned saint, an honourable villain!
O nature, what hadst thou to do in hell
When thou didst bower the spirit of a fiend
In mortal paradise of such sweet flesh?
Was ever book containing such vile matter
So fairly bound? O, that deceit should dwell
In such a gorgeous palace.

sentences.en: Oh, you have a snake's heart hidden by a beautiful face!
Did a dragon ever keep such a beautiful cave?
You are a beautiful tyrant and an angelic fiend.
You are a dove-feathered raven and a wolf-like lamb!
You are a hated thing hidden in a divine show!
You are the opposite of what you seem to be.
You are a damned saint and an honorable villain!
Oh, nature, why did you put the spirit of a demon in this mortal paradise of such sweet flesh?
Was there ever a book with such bad content bound so beautifully?
Oh, that such a lie should live in such a beautiful palace.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
There’s no trust,
No faith, no honesty in men. All perjur’d,
All forsworn, all naught, all dissemblers.
Ah, where’s my man? Give me some aqua vitae.
These griefs, these woes, these sorrows make me old.
Shame come to Romeo.

sentences.en: There is no trust.
There is no faith or honesty in men.
All are liars and all have broken their promises.
All are worthless and all are pretending to be something they are not.
Where is my man?
Give me some strong alcohol.
These problems and sorrows make me old.
Shame on Romeo.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Blister’d be thy tongue
For such a wish! He was not born to shame.
Upon his brow shame is asham’d to sit;
For ’tis a throne where honour may be crown’d
Sole monarch of the universal earth.
O, what a beast was I to chide at him!

sentences.en: May your tongue be blistered for such a wish!
He was not born for shame.
Shame would be ashamed to sit on his forehead.
It is a throne where honor can be crowned as the only ruler of the whole world.
Oh, what a beast was I to scold him!

speaker: NURSE
raw: Will you speak well of him that kill’d your cousin?

sentences.en: Will you speak well of the man who killed your cousin?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband?
Ah, poor my lord, what tongue shall smooth thy name,
When I thy three-hours’ wife have mangled it?
But wherefore, villain, didst thou kill my cousin?
That villain cousin would have kill’d my husband.
Back, foolish tears, back to your native spring,
Your tributary drops belong to woe,
Which you mistaking offer up to joy.
My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain,
And Tybalt’s dead, that would have slain my husband.
All this is comfort; wherefore weep I then?
Some word there was, worser than Tybalt’s death,
That murder’d me. I would forget it fain,
But O, it presses to my memory
Like damned guilty deeds to sinners’ minds.
Tybalt is dead, and Romeo banished.
That ‘banished,’ that one word ‘banished,’
Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt’s death
Was woe enough, if it had ended there.
Or if sour woe delights in fellowship,
And needly will be rank’d with other griefs,
Why follow’d not, when she said Tybalt’s dead,
Thy father or thy mother, nay or both,
Which modern lamentation might have mov’d?
But with a rear-ward following Tybalt’s death,
‘Romeo is banished’—to speak that word
Is father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet,
All slain, all dead. Romeo is banished,
There is no end, no limit, measure, bound,
In that word’s death, no words can that woe sound.
Where is my father and my mother, Nurse?

sentences.en: Should I speak badly of him who is my husband?
Oh, my poor husband!
Who will say good things about you now?
I, your wife of three hours, have attacked your name!
But why, villain, did you kill my cousin?
That villain cousin would have killed my husband.
Go away, foolish tears, and go back to your source.
Your drops belong to sadness, but you offer them to joy by mistake.
My husband, whom Tybalt wanted to kill, is alive.
And Tybalt, who wanted to kill my husband, is dead.
All of this is comfort, so why do I cry then?
Some word was worse than the death of Tybalt.
That word murdered me.
I would like to forget it, but oh, it stays in my memory.
It presses on me like guilty deeds press on sinners' minds.
Tybalt is dead, and Romeo is banished.
That one word 'banished' has killed ten thousand Tybalts.
Tybalt's death was enough sadness if it had ended there.
Perhaps sadness likes company.
Then why did the news of Tybalt's death not come with 'your father is dead,' or your mother, or both?
I would have cried for that in the normal way.
But because you followed Tybalt's death with 'Romeo is banished', speaking that word means everyone is killed.
Father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, and Juliet are all dead.
Romeo is banished.
There is no end or limit to the death in that word.
No words can describe that sadness.
Where are my father and my mother, Nurse?

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Weeping and wailing over Tybalt’s corse.
Will you go to them? I will bring you thither.

sentences.en: They are crying over Tybalt's body.
Will you go to them?
I will bring you there.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Wash they his wounds with tears. Mine shall be spent,
When theirs are dry, for Romeo’s banishment.
Take up those cords. Poor ropes, you are beguil’d,
Both you and I; for Romeo is exil’d.
He made you for a highway to my bed,
But I, a maid, die maiden-widowed.
Come cords, come Nurse, I’ll to my wedding bed,
And death, not Romeo, take my maidenhead.

sentences.en: Let them wash his wounds with tears.
My tears will flow for Romeo's banishment when theirs are dry.
Take up those ropes.
Poor ropes, you are tricked, both you and I, because Romeo is exiled.
He made you as a road to my bed.
But I will die a virgin widow.
Come ropes, come Nurse.
I will go to my wedding bed.
And death, not Romeo, will take my virginity.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Hie to your chamber. I’ll find Romeo
To comfort you. I wot well where he is.
Hark ye, your Romeo will be here at night.
I’ll to him, he is hid at Lawrence’ cell.

sentences.en: Hurry to your room.
I will find Romeo to comfort you.
I know well where he is.
Listen, your Romeo will be here tonight.
I will go to him.
He is hiding at the friar's cell.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
O find him, give this ring to my true knight,
And bid him come to take his last farewell.

sentences.en: Please find him.
Give this ring to my true knight.
Tell him to come and say his last goodbye.

raw: Exeunt.
